item.title: Yayoi Kusama dies at 97, weeks before Amsterdam show
item.description:
Yayoi Kusama dies at 97, weeks before Amsterdam show

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, whose polka dots, pumpkins and mirrored infinity rooms made her one of the world’s most famous contemporary artists, has died at the age of 97.

Her death comes just over two weeks before a major retrospective of her work opens at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, turning the show into a posthumous tribute.

From hallucinations to art
Born in Matsumoto in 1929, Kusama began drawing as a child, channelling troubling visions and hallucinations into the repeated nets, dots and other forms that would define her work. She moved to New York in the late 1950s and became a central figure in the city’s avant-garde art scene.

She returned to Japan in 1973 and, in 1977, voluntarily took up residence in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital, where she lived for the rest of her life while working daily in a studio nearby.

Amsterdam retrospective
The Stedelijk exhibition, which opens on September 11 and runs until January 17, is the final stop of a European tour that began at the Fondation Beyeler near Basel and passed through Cologne’s Museum Ludwig.

It brings together more than 300 works spanning over 70 years, including pieces never shown in Europe before and new installations made for the show.
“She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush,” her studio said.

item.title: Srebrenica war criminal Ratko Mladić dies in The Hague
item.description:
Srebrenica war criminal Ratko Mladić dies in The Hague

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, has died aged 84 in the United Nations detention unit in The Hague, a UN official has confirmed.

It was Mladić’s forces who overran Srebrenica – a UN “safe area” guarded by lightly armed Dutch peacekeepers known as Dutchbat – and killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in July 1995. It was the worst mass killing in Europe since the Second World War.

Mladić had been held in the UN detention unit in Scheveningen since his arrest in Serbia in 2011, after 16 years on the run. Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, he had been in poor health for years and reportedly suffered another stroke over the summer.

An international tribunal convicted him in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and jailed him for life; the verdict was upheld on appeal in 2021. He showed no remorse during his trial.

His death comes days after the tribunal rejected a request from his defence team, backed by the Serbian government, to release him on humanitarian grounds so he could spend his final days in Serbia.

Dutch guilt and apologies
For the Netherlands, the memory of Srebrenica is an open wound. Dutchbat’s failure to protect the victims led to a 2002 inquiry whose findings pushed the government at the time to resign, and to years of court action by survivors against the state.

Prime minister Mark Rutte apologised to Dutchbat veterans in 2022, saying they had been sent on an impossible mission and unfairly blamed for the killings. The government also repeated its “deepest apologies” to survivors in 2025.

Thousands gathered in Srebrenica to mark 30 years since the genocide last year. In the Netherlands, campaigners are still pressing for a national monument to the victims in The Hague.

item.title: Arsonists target planned asylum shelter for teen refugees
item.description:
Arsonists target planned asylum shelter for teen refugees

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Someone tried to set fire to a building in Valkenswaard in Noord-Brabant, which is being prepared as a shelter for teenage refugees, police have said.

The fire was started at two points on the former business premises on Leenderweg late on Wednesday, several windows were also broken.

Police said on Thursday that they were treating the incident as arson. A flammable liquid may have been thrown against the building, according to reports.

News emerged less than two weeks ago that COA, the refugee settlement agency, had approved a plan to house 40 unaccompanied minors aged 14 to 18 at the site for up to five years, a term that could be extended to 10.

Valkenswaard council stressed that no final decision had yet been taken, and that it would work through the details with COA over the coming months.

Run of attacks
The arson is the latest in a wave of vandalism, fires and bomb scares at sites earmarked for asylum seekers. In June, explosives were found at a planned centre in nearby Nuenen.

Earlier in the year, an explosion damaged a building in Den Bosch earmarked for teenage refugees, and a disused town hall in Loosdrecht was targeted during weeks of riots and arson.

The domestic security service AIVD is still investigating whether organised groups are behind the unrest.

item.title: Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell
item.description:
Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Small private landlords are selling off cheap, shared housing that students depend on, new figures from the land registry Kadaster show.

Across the Dutch cities with a university, these private landlords cut the number of homes they rent out by 19% on average over three years, according to NRC, which reported the figures.

Bigger property companies bought and built enough to keep the total number of rental homes almost steady, and student cities are attractive to investors, but these tend to be smaller studios rather than shared houses.

For a student hunting a room, that means there are likely fewer affordable shared rooms and more competition.

Hardest on internationals
International students are hardest hit by this, as they cannot join the years-long waiting lists for social housing, which the Kadaster figures don’t include, and often have to rent from abroad without seeing the room first.

That leaves them relying on the private market, which is shrinking, and more exposed to scams and overcharging.

It is not the same everywhere though – the number of rental homes actually rose in Amsterdam, Leiden and Eindhoven, while The Hague and Utrecht saw the steepest falls.

The national shortage stood at 21,500 rooms last year, and more students are giving up the search and staying with their parents, according to student housing centre Kences, which has linked the sell-off to lost rooms. Its next report is due on September 3.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan this week asked councils to be more flexible about shared student houses, after 10 students in Groningen faced eviction because their council would not treat them as one household.

item.title: Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors
item.description:
Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema wants to decriminalise sleeping outdoors, despite objections from residents of the Plantage neighbourhood in the east of the city.

Residents have launched a petition to prevent that from happening, according to AT5. Sleeping on the street or in parks is technically a fineable offence, although in practice no one has been fined over the past year. The mayor now wants it to become official policy.

Plantage resident Dennis de Vreede, who supports the petition, said he fears scrapping criminal liability will lead to more people sleeping outdoors, more nuisance and less possibilities for official action – despite acknowledging that fines are pointless.

“These people cannot afford it and might end up in even more debt trouble,” he told AT5. “But the entire legal framework collapses, meaning the police can no longer take action at all.”

“Shameful” fines

Halsema called fining sleeping homeless people “shameful” in 2021 and has said the measure doesn’t even work. “The intention is that the fine will bring about a change in behaviour,” she wrote, but she questioned whether it actually reduces nuisance.

From 2021 to 2024, fines were only issued for nuisance resulting from sleeping outdoors. Some 1,800 fines were handed out in that period.

But Bianca Koster of the Rainbow Group agrees that fining has little effect. “It helps to address the visibility, but not the core of the problem,” she said.

What needs to be addressed, she said, is why people end up on the streets. She called for more shelters, more care and more housing.

“I understand that when it gets visibly worse, people think we have to do something,” she said. “But punishing people is not the way.”

item.title: Back to the office: learning Dutch at work is the new perk
item.description:
Partner content

Back to the office: learning Dutch at work is the new perk

August 27, 2026

With working from home increasingly out of favour with employers, offering in-company Dutch courses can be a great way of getting your international staff back on location.  

Earlier this month financial services group ABN Amro said it wanted its staff to come into the office for at least three days a week. The move was necessary, the bank said, to increase creativity, encourage contacts between staff and improve the differentiation between their work and private lives. It would also, the bank said, make it easier to integrate new colleagues into their jobs.

It’s a trend that is becoming increasingly apparent across Dutch industry. After all, work is about more than just sitting at a desk or being part of an online meeting. It is about interacting with colleagues, sharing experiences and learning something new. And this is one reason why in-company language courses are growing in popularity. They help people to develop skills together while strengthening intra-team communications. And they are also proving a popular perk!

“We’ve noticed that an increasing number of companies are offering Dutch courses at their offices,” says Margreet van ‘t Haaff, owner of language school Taalthuis, which recently expanded to Amstelveen, Rotterdam and Eindhoven and now offers lessons in 10 different cities.

From online to in-company

Taalthuis pioneered the development of online lessons during the coronavirus pandemic and found an enthusiastic market for learning Dutch when people were confined to their homes. Now, however, in-company lessons are becoming increasingly popular as employers seek ways of improving contacts between staff – and helping their foreign workforce settle into the Netherlands more quickly.

“Employers see language lessons as a way of encouraging people to reduce the amount of time they work at home as well as to boost team spirit,” says Margreet. “It’s not a question of forcing people to go back to the office, but of making it more attractive to do so. And of course, learning Dutch helps you to feel more at home as well as getting to know your colleagues.”

Dutch as teamwork

Taalthuis’s dedicated teachers come to the company itself to provide the lessons – either 14-week courses tailored to fit their students’ language level, or tailor-made conversation sessions to meet a particular need on a month-by-month basis. Every student is given a test to find out their Dutch level before they start.

The courses themselves cover beginners to C1 and emphasise conversation skills, which, says Margreet, are perfect for boosting chats between colleagues over lunch or during brainstorming sessions.

The lessons include discussion about typical Dutch themes such as Koningsdag, cycling culture and, of course, food. You will learn about the delights of bitterballen at the vrijmibo, and how to explain your disappointment to your colleagues when faced with a broodje kaas for lunch in the bedrijfsrestaurant.

Learn Dutch during office hours

Many classroom-based Dutch courses take place during office hours, and people who have been struggling to learn Dutch often say that they find it difficult to combine work with lessons and family duties. Offering lessons at the office is another way of getting round that hurdle.

One Taalthuis client, for example, offers its workers lunch combined with a Dutch language course. Others offer lessons towards the end of the day, but in company time, such as a session at 4.30pm, allowing staff to still go home at 6.15pm.

Engineering group Haskoning began offering Taalthuis language courses to its employees in Delft about two years ago and continues to do so. “We recognised a growing need among our international colleagues in the Netherlands to feel more integrated into Dutch society and workplace culture,” says Sofia Aguero from the company’s HR department.

Strengthening teamwork

“From a company perspective the Taalthuis courses strengthen team cohesion, support retention, and enhance our inclusive culture. And given all the positive feedback from students and a growing interest from other employees, we’re already planning future sessions and exploring ways to expand access.”

“Learning Dutch makes it more fun to go to the gym or to have a chat with your colleagues at the coffee machine,” says Taalthuis teacher Floortje, who specialises in in-company courses. “You can talk about the weather, your weekend, what you want to drink… it just makes it easier to have personal contact.”

If you are an employer who would like to offer your staff Dutch lessons, feel free to contact Taalthuis. And if you are a worker who would like your company to offer Dutch lessons at the office, ask your HR department to get in touch.

item.title: Heavy thunderstorms expected this evening
item.description:
Heavy thunderstorms expected this evening

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Following Thursday’s oppressive daytime humidity and heat – with temperatures ranging between 25° and 30° – the night will see rain and thunderstorms in the south of the country moving north, reports the KNMI weather service.

“During the showers, wind gusts of up to 60 km/h are possible,” said the weather service, and “there is a chance of hail up to 2 cm and heavy rain may fall in a short time”.

While no official warnings have currently been issued, KNMI said there’s a possibility of wind gusts, downed trees and local flooding.

The weather service has just launched a thunderstorm notification app to alert people of local storms happening within 15 minutes of where they are. Currently operating as a beta test through August 31 in the KNMI app, you can download it here and provide feedback later.

item.title: New agreement secures healthcare for 20,000 refugee children
item.description:
New agreement secures healthcare for 20,000 refugee children

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The national refugee settlement agency COA has secured a three-year contract with public health body GGD to ensure that the nearly 20,000 children living in Dutch asylum centres will continue to receive uninterrupted healthcare.

The current contract was due to expire in October while another with a separate health body wouldn’t come into effect until June 2027, leaving a potential 8-month gap that led six children’s ombudsmen to brand “a serious violation of children’s rights”.

“The decision to award GGD GHOR Nederland a new three-year contract brings stability and clarity,” said André Rouvoet, chairman of GGD GHOR Nederland.

“Accessible youth healthcare is of great importance for asylum-seeking children. With this period, we can continue to do what is necessary: ​​provide accessible, expert, and preventive care.”

Children’s rights organizations were concerned that a gap in care could lead to lower levels of vaccination and a decrease in flagging health and mental health issues.

While regular medical and emergency care are available to refugees, without the new funding, preventative care – which also includes consultations, growth checks and developmental assessments – could have fallen through the cracks.

item.title: New funding for long Covid research centre raised
item.description:
New funding for long Covid research centre raised

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Long COVID Foundation (SLC) has launched a National Research & Innovation Center to investigate long covid in the Netherlands as government money has dried up.

With some €40 million the government provided for research having been spent and no new budget yet allocated, the foundation awarded €500,000 to seven researchers to keep their research going and to “translate scientific discoveries more quickly into diagnostics and targeted treatments for adults and children.”

“SLC wants to prevent years of investment, knowledge and research power from being lost.”

The money is being given to researchers from the hospitals Amsterdam UMC, the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, UMC Utrecht and Erasmus MC. The foundation’s goal is that the centre, operating as an independent foundation and an open national research network, will be a central hub for stimulating and linking research under one national program.

Still no treatment

Calling long covid “one of the great unresolved medical challenges of our time”, the foundation estimates 400,000 people have been affected by it – 100,000 of them seriously. “Yet there are no proven healing treatment, effective diagnostics and targeted therapies yet.”

Long covid sufferers struggle with fatigue, brain fog, loss of concentration, and memory and immune system problems that have severely limited their ability to work and lead normal lives.

Targeted treatments

The foundation says it’s becoming increasingly clear that long covid suffers can be distinguished by groups. “An important task for the centre will be to better distinguish these groups and to investigate which treatments can work in which patients.”

The foundation is also looking into other the post-acute infection syndromes, such as ME/CFS, a chronic illness characterised by an inability to function.

In the future, says SLC, “long-term public and private financing is also needed”.

“The stronger and more structural the research is organized, the more likely it is that scientific discoveries will lead to the diagnostics and targeted treatments that patients have been waiting for so long.”

item.title: Summer 2026 was Netherlands’ hottest ever recorded
item.description:
Summer 2026 was Netherlands’ hottest ever recorded

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The summer of 2026 was the warmest in the Netherlands since national records began in 1901, figures from the KNMI weather service show.

The average temperature at the KNMI’s benchmark station in De Bilt reached 19.3° over the three summer months, beating the previous record (set in 2018) of 18.9° by nearly half a degree. With August almost over, the record is already beyond reach, broadcaster NOS reported.

In June the KNMI issued its first-ever code red warning for extreme heat, a level not triggered even during the record temperatures of 2019. The country then went through multiple heatwaves, and the public health institute RIVM has linked at least 900 excess deaths to the June spell alone.

The nights were also extremely hot. In Maastricht, the temperature stayed above 22° for three nights running for the first time, which has never been recorded anywhere in the Netherlands before, even over two nights.

Peter Siegmund, a climate expert at the KNMI, told NOS that a summer this warm can now be expected roughly once every five years in the current climate – an interval he expects to shorten as warming continues.

Under the KNMI’s highest climate scenario, he said, a summer of this kind would be an average one by around 2050.
